t: Medicare Open Enrollment: Here’s What’s Changing, and What Mistakes To Avoid

p: Annual open enrollment is underway for Medicare, the federal program that provides health insurance to roughly
. The coverage choices are complex and often consequential.

Medicare provides health insurance to people 65 or older, as well as to some younger people with disabilities or certain health conditions. But it isn’t one plan. It’s more like a build-your-own-insurance menu.

Roughly half of beneficiaries are enrolled in traditional Medicare, which consists of Parts A and B. Administered by the federal government, the plan covers hospital stays, skilled nursing care, doctor visits, outpatient care, and preventive screenings. Enrollees can typically see any healthcare provider who accepts Medicare, and they rarely need approval for diagnostic tests, such as MRIs and CT scans. However, there’s no cap on out-of-pocket expenses in traditional Medicare, and it doesn’t cover most prescriptions or dental, vision, or hearing services.
As a result, most traditional Medicare enrollees buy extra coverage from private insurance companies under
, the prescription drug plan. Some also buy a Medigap policy that covers the costs traditional Medicare leaves behind, such as deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance.
This year, the

of Medicare beneficiaries opted for privately offered, all-in-one managed-care plans known as Medicare Advantage, usually including prescription drug coverage, dental, and vision. The drawbacks are smaller networks and a greater likelihood that treatments and medications will require prior authorization. Like beneficiaries in traditional Medicare, Medicare Advantage participants also pay Part B premiums.
“People really need to do their research before they enroll in Medicare, because there are trade-offs,” said
, a co-director at the Center for Medicare Advocacy.

Every fall, insurers that offer Part D and Advantage plans send enrollees a critical document known as an Annual Notice of Change. It’s a cheat sheet outlining what will be different in the following year: premiums, deductibles, covered drugs. Consumer advocates and Medicare experts say people sometimes make the costly mistake of throwing it out or filing it away without reading it. Can’t find it? Call the insurer and ask for another copy.

Juliette Cubanski, who directs the Program on Medicare Policy at KFF, said people who don’t shop around could be leaving money on the table.
“It is worth it to avoid any unpleasant surprises in the form of either higher premiums or higher cost sharing for covered services in 2027,” she said.

Those who want to stay in Medicare Advantage must select new coverage, or they’ll be moved to traditional Medicare automatically. For those shopping for a new plan, low monthly premiums may be appealing, but it’s important to read the fine print and add up the other costs.

“There are going to be, often, increases in cost sharing and copays, increases in out-of-pocket caps, and reductions in the scope of some of the extra benefits that Medicare Advantage plans provide,” Lipschutz said.
So ask: Is my prescription covered? Is my pharmacy preferred? Is my doctor in-network? What does the dental benefit actually cover?
And pay attention to the out-of-pocket maximum for the Advantage plans, Cubanski said, so you know how much you might have to shell out in 2027.
“Look at that dollar value specifically,” she said.

For those moving to traditional Medicare, it won’t come with a drug plan, so enrollees must sign up for a new Part D plan if they want most prescriptions covered. Enrollees who miss that step when they are first eligible may not have drug coverage for the coming year, and they may face a
on their monthly premiums for life.

When selecting a drug plan, enrollees must also tell their insurer how they want to pay, either by getting a bill in the mail or by having the cost deducted from their Social Security. If you don’t pick a payment plan, you could get dropped from coverage.

If enrollees elect to leave their Medicare Advantage plans for traditional Medicare within their first year of joining Medicare, they have a guaranteed right to buy a Medigap plan, with no health screening. Medicare experts advise enrollees to write down all their prescription drugs, as well as any procedures planned in the next year, such as a joint replacement or dental work, to help them decide which plan will cover their needs. Call a favorite doctor’s office to see whether they are in-network for the plans being considered. Remember that brokers might earn commissions, especially on Advantage plans, and might not represent every plan.
